Although the wording does not require this, the meaning does, since one does not swear by an indefinite thing whose identity is unknown. When a general sense is intended, the definite is included within it, and so the oath is fitting. Similarly, what comes in this kind of indefinite form should be understood in the same way, such as His saying: ﴿By the Mount and a written Book﴾ [At-Tur: 1]. And when ﴿a written Book﴾ [At-Tur: 2] is understood in a general sense, two meanings are included: the divine books, such as the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an. Then the oath by it is fitting.

When He mentioned ﴿the promised Day﴾, which is by agreement the Day of Resurrection, and this was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), it was fitting that what is sworn by should be those who witness on that Day and those who are witnessed against (p-450), if *shahid* means witnessing. It was promised and then became witnessed. The opinions of the exegetes differ regarding the identification of these two.

From Ibn ʿAbbas also and al-Hasan: the witness is the Day of ʿArafah and the Day of Friday, and in each of them there is a witnessed Day, which is the Day of Resurrection. From Abu Malik: Jesus, and ﴿witnessed﴾ is his community. From ʿAli: the Day of ʿArafah, and ﴿witnessed﴾ is the Day of Nahr. From al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim: the guardian angels, and ﴿witnessed﴾ against them are the people. From ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya: Muhammad, and (witnessed) against him is his community. From him also: the prophets, and ﴿witnessed﴾ are their nations. From Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil: the limbs on the Day of Resurrection, and ﴿witnessed﴾ are their owners. It was said: they are Monday and Friday. It was said: the angels who follow one another, and the Dawn Qur'an (recitation). It was said: the star, the night and the day. It was said: God, the angels and the people of knowledge, and what is witnessed is the Oneness (of God), and ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al ʿImran: 19]. It was said: His creatures, the exalted, and ﴿witnessed﴾ by it is His Oneness. It was said: they are the Black Stone and the pilgrims. It was said: the nights, the days and the children of Adam. It was said: the prophets and Muhammad. These are twenty-seven opinions, and each has a basis. The Sufis have opinions other than these. The apparent meaning is what we said at first.

As for the response to the oath, it was said to be omitted. It was said: it is ﴿You will surely be resurrected﴾ or the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is indicated by ﴿Cursed were the people of the trench﴾. It was also said: the response is stated, and it was said it is ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted﴾ [Al-Buruj: 10]. Al-Mubarrad said it is ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾ [Al-Buruj: 12]. It was said it is (qutila, "were cursed"), and this is what we choose, with the lam omitted, meaning: "Surely cursed were the people of the trench." Its omission is good, as it is good in His saying: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [Ash-Shams: 1], then He said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [Ash-Shams: 9], meaning: "Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies it." When (qutila) is the response to the oath, it is a declarative sentence. It was said it is a supplication, so the response is other than it. Al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam read it with the shaddah (quttila), while the majority read it with the lighter form (qutila).

Al-Rabi', Abu al-'Aliyah, and Ibn Ishaq said: God sent a wind upon the believers, which seized their souls, or something similar to this. The fire came out and burned the disbelievers who were on the two edges of the trench. According to this view, the word "killed" (qutila) is meant literally and not in the sense of "cursed." It is a report of what God did to the disbelievers and to those who wanted to tempt the believers away from their religion. The view of these scholars contradicts the view of the majority (al-jumhur) and what the narratives they mentioned indicate.

The majority read ﴿al-nari﴾ (the fire) in the genitive case (al-nari بِالجَرِّ), and it is a badal ishtimal (a substitute expressing inclusion, a grammatical apposition in which the substitute is related to what it replaces by a relationship other than identity), or a badal kull min kull (a substitute that is wholly identical to what it replaces) with an elided element estimated, meaning "the trench of the fire." A group read ﴿al-naru﴾ (the fire) in the nominative case. It was said: this is according to the meaning of their killing, and the People of the Trench in that case would be the believers, and they were killed in their literal sense.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Haywa, and Isa read ﴿al-waqudi﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5) with a damma on the waw, and it is a verbal noun (masdar). The majority read it with a fatha, and it refers to that which is kindled with it (fuel). Sibawayh has related that the fatha reading is also a masdar, like the damma reading.

Apparently the pronoun in ﴿idh hum﴾ (when they) refers to those who burn the believers. Likewise, in ﴿wa-hum﴾ (and they), according to the opinion of al-Rabi', it refers to the disbelievers, and ﴿hum﴾ also refers back to them. The meaning of ﴿ʿala ma yafʿalun﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, at what they do) is what they intend to do of their deeds against the believers.

It was also said: "The People of the Trench" is a complete sentence (mubtada'), and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿dhat al-waqud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5, possessor of the fuel). The intended meaning of His saying "and they" is the Quraysh who used to tempt the believing men and women. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is governed by "was killed" (qutila), meaning they were cursed and sat by the fire, or by what was near it from the edges of the trench, as al-A'sha said:

Kindled for two cold-stricken men who warm themselves by it,
And the dew and the shaved-headed one spent the night by the fire.

﴿shuhud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, witnesses) means that some of them bear witness for others before the king, that is, that he did not neglect what he was commanded to do. Or it means witnesses on the Day of Resurrection to what they did to the believers, on the day when their limbs will testify against them about their deeds.

The majority read ﴿naqamu﴾ (they held against) with a fatha on the qaf. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a kasra, meaning they did not criticize or deny faith, as in His saying: ﴿Do you hold anything against us except that we believed in God?﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:59), and as in the words of Qays al-Ruqayyat:

They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah except
That they are forbearing when they become angry.

They made what was in the extreme of beauty ugly, to the point that they held it against him, as the poet said:

There is no fault in them except the squint of their eyes,
And so are the noble birds, their eyes are squinting.

In al-Muntakhab: He said ﴿illa an yu'minu﴾ (except that they believe, al-Buruj 85:8) because the punishment was only inflicted upon faith in the future. If they disbelieved in the future, they would not be punished for what passed. It is as if He said: "except that they persist in their faith." End of quotation. He mentioned the attributes by which God deserves to be believed in: that He is Mighty (Aziz), Overpowering (Ghalib), Capable (Qadir), whose punishment is feared; Praiseworthy (Hamid), Bestower of blessings, to whom praise is due for His blessing; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them is rightly obligated to worship Him and humble himself before Him, as an affirmation, because what they held against them is the truth that only a falsifier immersed in error holds against.

﴿And God is Witness over everything﴾ (al-Buruj 85:9) is a threat to them, meaning He knows what they did, so He will requite them. The apparent meaning is that ﴿those who tempted﴾ (al-Buruj 85:10) is general, covering everyone who afflicted the believing men and women with torture or harm, and that for them are two punishments: a punishment for their disbelief and a punishment for their temptation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by "those who tempted" he means the People of the Trench specifically, and by "those who believed" those thrown into the trench. The meaning of "they tempted them" is that they tormented them with fire and burned them. ﴿For them﴾ (al-Buruj 85:10), in the Hereafter, is ﴿the punishment of Hell﴾ for their disbelief, ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾, which is another great fire that spreads as a conflagration spreads. Or, for them is the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter, and for them is the punishment of the Burning in this world, because it is related that the fire turned back upon them and burned them. End of quotation.

It seems that what he permitted should not be allowed, because the verse says ﴿then they did not repent﴾ (al-Buruj 85:10), and it has not been transmitted to us that any of those burners repented. Rather, the apparent meaning is that they were not cursed except that they had already died in disbelief.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿then they did not repent﴾ strengthens the view that the verses refer to the Quraysh, because this expression applies to the Quraysh more appropriately than to those who are known to have died in their disbelief. As for the Quraysh, among them at the time the verse was revealed were those who repented and believed. End of quotation.

Likewise, His saying ﴿Indeed those who believed﴾ (al-Buruj 85:10) is meant in its generality, not as referring to those thrown into the fire. ﴿al-batsh﴾ (the seizing) means taking with force. ﴿He originates and repeats﴾ (al-Buruj 85:13). Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said: He originates creation by bringing it into existence, and repeats it by resurrection (al-hashr). Ibn Abbas said: it is general over all things, meaning everything that is originated and everything that is repeated. Al-Tabari said: He originates the punishment and repeats it upon the disbelievers. Similar to this is reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: the fire consumes them until they become charcoal, then He returns them as a new creation. It has been read ﴿yabda'u﴾ (he begins) from the triliteral root bada'a, related by Abu Zayd.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: the one who shows affection to His servants through forgiveness. And I ride in the battle, a naked woman, [a camel] submissive in mating, a milk-giving one, and loving (wadud).

That is, she has no offspring toward whom she yearns. It was also said: al-Wadud is on the pattern fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, like rakub (ridden) and halub (milked), meaning His righteous servants love Him.

Al-Qaffal said: ﴿Possessor of the Throne﴾ means possessor of dominion and authority. End of quotation.

Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, al-Mufaddal from Asim, and the two Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read ﴿al-majid﴾ (Glorious) with a kasra on the dal, as an attribute of the Throne. Its majd (glory) is its greatness, its height, its magnitude, the beauty of its form, and its composition, for it was said: the Throne is the most beautiful of bodies in form and composition. Whoever reads ﴿dhi al-Arsh﴾ with a ya' may take ﴿al-majid﴾ in the genitive as an attribute of dhi. The better view is to make these nominative words predicates of huwa, so that ﴿fa'al﴾ (the doer) is the predicate. It is also permissible that ﴿al-Wadud dhu al-Arsh﴾ are two attributes of the Forgiving, and ﴿fa'al﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject, and the form fa''al is used because what He wills and does is in utmost abundance. The meaning is that whatever His will is attached to, He does, and nothing opposes Him.

﴿Has the account of the hosts reached you?﴾ (al-Buruj 85:17) is an affirmation of the state of the disbelievers, meaning: their account has already reached you, and what happened to them with their prophets, and the punishments that befell them because of their denial. Likewise, the punishments of Quraysh will be like what befell them. Al-junud means the masses prepared for battle. ﴿Pharaoh and Thamud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:18) is a substitute for "the hosts," and it seems to be by elision of a modifier, meaning the hosts of Pharaoh. What happened to them is abbreviated because they are mentioned in more than one surah of the Qur'an. Thamud is mentioned because their story was famous in the land of the Arabs and they are earlier. Pharaoh is mentioned because his story was famous among the People of the Book and also among the pre-Islamic Arabs. Do you not see Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma and his saying:

Did you not see that God destroyed Tubba',
And destroyed Luqman ibn 'Ad and 'Adiyy?

And destroyed Dhu al-Qarnayn, from before he turned away,
And Pharaoh, the tyrant who transgressed, and the Najashi?

Pharaoh was among the later ones in destruction, so by mentioning his story and the story of Thamud, He indicated similar accounts of the nations that denied and their destruction.

﴿Rather, those who disbelieved﴾ (al-Buruj 85:19), that is, from among your people, ﴿are in denial﴾, out of envy toward you, not taking a lesson from what befell those before them when they denied their prophets.

﴿And God is encompassing them from behind﴾ (al-Buruj 85:20), that is, He is capable of bringing upon them what He brought upon Pharaoh and Thamud and those who were encompassed by Him. So He is confined in utmost restriction, unable to repel it. The meaning is: their destruction is near. When He mentioned that they are in denial, and that denial has overwhelmed them until it became like a container for them, and since they denied him (ﷺ) and denied what he brought, which is the Qur'an, God informed about what they denied, saying: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ (al-Buruj 85:21), that is, rather, what they denied is a glorious Qur'an. Its majd is its nobility over all other books through its inimitability in its composition, the soundness of its meanings, its reporting of unseen matters, and other excellences.

The majority read ﴿Qur'anun majid﴾ with the Qur'an described as the qualified noun and the adjective as qualifier. Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿Qur'anu majidin﴾ in the idafah (construct) form. Ibn Khalawayh said: I heard Ibn al-Anbari say its meaning is: "rather, it is the Qur'an of a glorious Lord," as the poet said:

But the wealth is a forgiving Lord (rabb ghafur).

Its meaning is: but the wealth is the wealth of a forgiving Lord. End of quotation. On this, al-Zamakhshari took it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Yamani read ﴿Qur'anun majid﴾ in the idafah form, and that God Most High is the Glorious One. End of quotation. It is also permissible that it is of the construction of a qualified noun to its qualifier, so that its referent and the referent of the tanwin and the nominative case of "majid" are one. This is preferable, for the two readings agree.

The majority read ﴿fi lawhin﴾ (in a tablet) with a fatha on the lam, and ﴿mahfuz﴾ (preserved) in the genitive as an attribute of "lawh." The preserved tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) is the one in which all things are contained. Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn al-Sumayqa read it with a damma on the lam. Ibn Khalawayh said: al-lawh means the air. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the tablet above the seventh heaven, which is the preserved tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) from the reaching of the devils to it. End of quotation. Al-A'raj, Zayd ibn Ali, Ibn Mahisin, and Nafi' in one transmission from him read ﴿mahfuzun﴾ in the nominative as an attribute of "Qur'an," as God Most High said: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ (al-Hijr 15:9), meaning it is preserved in hearts, and no error or alteration reaches it.

A group read ﴿al-naru﴾ (the fire) in the nominative case. It was also said: "The People of the Trench" is a complete sentence (mubtada'), and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿dhat al-waqud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5, possessor of the fuel). The intended meaning of His saying "and they" is the Quraysh who used to tempt the believing men and women. Kindled for two cold-stricken men who warm themselves by it,
And the dew and the shaved-headed one spent the night by the fire.

﴿shuhud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, witnesses) means that some of them bear witness for others before the king, that is, that he did not neglect what he was commanded to do. Or it means witnesses on the Day of Resurrection to what they did to the believers, on the day when their limbs will testify against them about their deeds.

The majority read ﴿naqamu﴾ (they held against) with a fatha on the qaf. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a kasra, meaning they did not criticize or deny faith, as in His saying: ﴿Do you hold anything against us except that we believed in God?﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:59), and as in the words of Qays al-Ruqayyat:

They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah except
That they are forbearing when they become angry.

They made what was in the extreme of beauty ugly, to the point that they held it against him, as the poet said:

There is no fault in them except the squint of their eyes,
And so are the noble birds, their eyes are squinting.

In al-Muntakhab: He said ﴿illa an yu'minu﴾ (except that they believe, al-Buruj 85:8) because the punishment was only inflicted upon faith in the future. If they disbelieved in the future, they would not be punished for what passed. It is as if He said: "except that they persist in their faith." End of quotation. He mentioned the attributes by which God deserves to be believed in: that He is Mighty (Aziz), Overpowering (Ghalib), Capable (Qadir), whose punishment is feared; Praiseworthy (Hamid), Bestower of blessings, to whom praise is due for His blessing; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them is rightly obligated to worship Him and humble himself before Him, as an affirmation, because what they held against them is the truth that only a falsifier immersed in error holds against.

And destroyed Luqman ibn 'Ad and 'Adiyy?

And Pharaoh, the tyrant who transgressed, and the Najashi?

A group read ﴿al-naru﴾ (the fire) in the nominative case. It was also said: "The People of the Trench" is a complete sentence (mubtada'), and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿dhat al-waqud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5, possessor of the fuel). The intended meaning of His saying "and they" is the Quraysh who used to tempt the believing men and women. Kindled for two cold-stricken men who warm themselves by it,
And the dew and the shaved-headed one spent the night by the fire.

﴿shuhud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, witnesses) means that some of them bear witness for others before the king, that is, that he did not neglect what he was commanded to do. Or it means witnesses on the Day of Resurrection to what they did to the believers, on the day when their limbs will testify against them about their deeds.

The majority read ﴿naqamu﴾ (they held against) with a fatha on the qaf. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a kasra, meaning they did not criticize or deny faith, as in His saying: ﴿Do you hold anything against us except that we believed in God?﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:59), and as in the words of Qays al-Ruqayyat:

They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah except
That they are forbearing when they become angry.

They made what was in the extreme of beauty ugly, to the point that they held it against him, as the poet said:

There is no fault in them except the squint of their eyes,
And so are the noble birds, their eyes are squinting.

In al-Muntakhab: He said ﴿illa an yu'minu﴾ (except that they believe, al-Buruj 85:8) because the punishment was only inflicted upon faith in the future. If they disbelieved in the future, they would not be punished for what passed. It is as if He said: "except that they persist in their faith." End of quotation. He mentioned the attributes by which God deserves to be believed in: that He is Mighty (Aziz), Overpowering (Ghalib), Capable (Qadir), whose punishment is feared; Praiseworthy (Hamid), Bestower of blessings, to whom praise is due for His blessing; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them is rightly obligated to worship Him and humble himself before Him, as an affirmation, because what they held against them is the truth that only a falsifier immersed in error holds against.

And destroyed Luqman ibn 'Ad and 'Adiyy?

And Pharaoh, the tyrant who transgressed, and the Najashi?

A group read ﴿al-naru﴾ (the fire) in the nominative case. It was also said: "The People of the Trench" is a complete sentence (mubtada'), and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿dhat al-waqud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5, possessor of the fuel). The intended meaning of His saying "and they" is the Quraysh who used to tempt the believing men and women. Kindled for two cold-stricken men who warm themselves by it,
And the dew and the shaved-headed one spent the night by the fire.

﴿shuhud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, witnesses) means that some of them bear witness for others before the king, that is, that he did not neglect what he was commanded to do. Or it means witnesses on the Day of Resurrection to what they did to the believers, on the day when their limbs will testify against them about their deeds.

The majority read ﴿naqamu﴾ (they held against) with a fatha on the qaf. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a kasra, meaning they did not criticize or deny faith, as in His saying: ﴿Do you hold anything against us except that we believed in God?﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:59), and as in the words of Qays al-Ruqayyat:

They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah except
That they are forbearing when they become angry.

They made what was in the extreme of beauty ugly, to the point that they held it against him, as the poet said:

There is no fault in them except the squint of their eyes,
And so are the noble birds, their eyes are squinting.

In al-Muntakhab: He said ﴿illa an yu'minu﴾ (except that they believe, al-Buruj 85:8) because the punishment was only inflicted upon faith in the future. If they disbelieved in the future, they would not be punished for what passed. It is as if He said: "except that they persist in their faith." End of quotation. He mentioned the attributes by which God deserves to be believed in: that He is Mighty (Aziz), Overpowering (Ghalib), Capable (Qadir), whose punishment is feared; Praiseworthy (Hamid), Bestower of blessings, to whom praise is due for His blessing; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them is rightly obligated to worship Him and humble himself before Him, as an affirmation, because what they held against them is the truth that only a falsifier immersed in error holds against.

And destroyed Luqman ibn 'Ad and 'Adiyy?

And Pharaoh, the tyrant who transgressed, and the Najashi?

A group read ﴿al-naru﴾ (the fire) in the nominative case. It was also said: "The People of the Trench" is a complete sentence (mubtada'), and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿dhat al-waqud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5, possessor of the fuel). The intended meaning of His saying "and they" is the Quraysh who used to tempt the believing men and women. Kindled for two cold-stricken men who warm themselves by it,
And the dew and the shaved-headed one spent the night by the fire.

﴿shuhud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, witnesses) means that some of them bear witness for others before the king, that is, that he did not neglect what he was commanded to do. Or it means witnesses on the Day of Resurrection to what they did to the believers, on the day when their limbs will testify against them about their deeds.

The majority read ﴿naqamu﴾ (they held against) with a fatha on the qaf. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a kasra, meaning they did not criticize or deny faith, as in His saying: ﴿Do you hold anything against us except that we believed in God?﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:59), and as in the words of Qays al-Ruqayyat:

They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah except
That they are forbearing when they become angry.

They made what was in the extreme of beauty ugly, to the point that they held it against him, as the poet said:

There is no fault in them except the squint of their eyes,
And so are the noble birds, their eyes are squinting.

In al-Muntakhab: He said ﴿illa an yu'minu﴾ (except that they believe, al-Buruj 85:8) because the punishment was only inflicted upon faith in the future. If they disbelieved in the future, they would not be punished for what passed. It is as if He said: "except that they persist in their faith." End of quotation. He mentioned the attributes by which God deserves to be believed in: that He is Mighty (Aziz), Overpowering (Ghalib), Capable (Qadir), whose punishment is feared; Praiseworthy (Hamid), Bestower of blessings, to whom praise is due for His blessing; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them is rightly obligated to worship Him and humble himself before Him, as an affirmation, because what they held against them is the truth that only a falsifier immersed in error holds against.

And destroyed Luqman ibn 'Ad and 'Adiyy?

And Pharaoh, the tyrant who transgressed, and the Najashi?

A group read ﴿al-naru﴾ (the fire) in the nominative case. It was also said: "The People of the Trench" is a complete sentence (mubtada'), and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿dhat al-waqud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:5, possessor of the fuel). The intended meaning of His saying "and they" is the Quraysh who used to tempt the believing men and women. Kindled for two cold-stricken men who warm themselves by it,
And the dew and the shaved-headed one spent the night by the fire.

﴿shuhud﴾ (al-Buruj 85:7, witnesses) means that some of them bear witness for others before the king, that is, that he did not neglect what he was commanded to do. Or it means witnesses on the Day of Resurrection to what they did to the believers, on the day when their limbs will testify against them about their deeds.

The majority read ﴿naqamu﴾ (they held against) with a fatha on the qaf. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a kasra, meaning they did not criticize or deny faith, as in His saying: ﴿Do you hold anything against us except that we believed in God?﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:59), and as in the words of Qays al-Ruqayyat:

They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah except
That they are forbearing when they become angry.

They made what was in the extreme of beauty ugly, to the point that they held it against him, as the poet said:

There is no fault in them except the squint of their eyes,
And so are the noble birds, their eyes are squinting.

In al-Muntakhab: He said ﴿illa an yu'minu﴾ (except that they believe, al-Buruj 85:8) because the punishment was only inflicted upon faith in the future. If they disbelieved in the future, they would not be punished for what passed. It is as if He said: "except that they persist in their faith." End of quotation. He mentioned the attributes by which God deserves to be believed in: that He is Mighty (Aziz), Overpowering (Ghalib), Capable (Qadir), whose punishment is feared; Praiseworthy (Hamid), Bestower of blessings, to whom praise is due for His blessing; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whoever is in them is rightly obligated to worship Him and humble himself before Him, as an affirmation, because what they held against them is the truth that only a falsifier immersed in error holds against.

And destroyed Luqman ibn 'Ad and 'Adiyy?

And Pharaoh, the tyrant who transgressed, and the Najashi?

Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the tablet above the seventh heaven, which is the preserved tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) from the reaching of the devils to it. End of quotation. Al-A'raj, Zayd ibn Ali, Ibn Mahisin, and Nafi' in one transmission from him read ﴿mahfuzun﴾ in the nominative as an attribute of "Qur'an," as God Most High said: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ (al-Hijr 15:9), meaning it is preserved in hearts, and no error or alteration reaches it.
